title: Open Problem (induced st-path of excess length three)
statement_text: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm to test whether a graph contains an induced path between specified vertices $s, t$ of length at least three more than the shortest $st$-path?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, and the length of a path is its number of edges. Given two vertices $s,t$ of a graph $G$, the question is whether $G$ has an induced path from $s$ to $t$ whose length exceeds the distance between $s$ and $t$ by at least three. Berger, Spirkl and Seymour (Seymour being a co-author of this paper) have a polynomial-time algorithm to test whether there is an induced $st$-path longer than the shortest $st$-path (i.e. of excess at least one). The authors mention, as related work on detecting long induced subgraphs of specific type, that the corresponding problem for excess at least three is open. The paper itself gives, for every fixed $\ell\ge5$, a polynomial-time algorithm testing whether a graph has an odd hole (induced cycle of length at least four) of length at least $\ell$.
notes: Stated in passing as 'It is open whether...' with no formal label. Arises from related work by Berger, Spirkl, and Seymour; one of the present paper's authors (Seymour) is involved in the related work.

title: Informal Conjecture (heavy path extension)
statement_text: If $C$ is a shortest long odd hole in a graph $G$ and $M$ is a set of $C$-major vertices such that one vertex of $M$ is nonadjacent to all the others, then there exists a path of $C$ of bounded length such that every vertex of $M$ has a neighbour in that path.
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, $|G|$ is the number of vertices of $G$, and the length of a path or cycle is its number of edges. A hole of $G$ is an induced subgraph that is a cycle of length at least four. Throughout, $\ell\ge5$ is a fixed integer, and a long path or hole is one of length at least $\ell$. If $C$ is a hole of $G$, a vertex $v\in V(G)\setminus V(C)$ is $C$-major if there is no three-vertex path of $C$ containing all the neighbours of $v$ in $V(C)$; $C$ is clean if no vertex is $C$-major. A shortest long odd hole is a long odd hole of minimum length. Bounded length means bounded by a constant depending only on $\ell$. The authors give a polynomial-time algorithm to test for a long odd hole, using the cleaning method: one generates polynomially many sets $X$ such that, if $G$ has a long odd hole, some $X$ contains all $C$-major vertices of a shortest long odd hole $C$ and no vertex of $C$. In the earlier odd hole detection algorithm (the case without the length constraint), the cleaning list relied on a theorem that if $C$ is a shortest odd hole and $M$ is a set of $C$-major vertices such that one vertex of $M$ is nonadjacent to all the others, then $C$ has a heavy edge $uv$, i.e. every vertex of $M$ is adjacent to $u$ or $v$. The authors tried to extend this to shortest long odd holes, where a heavy path of $C$ of bounded length would serve just as well; they say this extension might be true but they were unable to prove it, and instead prove that there is a bounded set of paths of $C$, each of bounded length, such that every vertex of $M$ has a neighbour in one of them, and only when the exceptional vertex of $M$ is carefully chosen.
notes: Stated as 'this extension might be true, but we were unable to prove it.' No formal labelled environment. PDF source — math notation may be partially garbled.

title: Open Question (running time improvement for long hole detection)
statement_text: Can the running times of $O(|G|^{\ell+1})$ for detecting a long hole and $O(|G|^{20\ell+40})$ for detecting a long odd hole — both $|G|^{O(\ell)}$ — be substantially improved for fixed $\ell$?
context_text: Graphs are finite and simple, $|G|$ is the number of vertices of $G$, and the length of a path or cycle is its number of edges. A hole of $G$ is an induced subgraph that is a cycle of length at least four. Throughout, $\ell\ge5$ is a fixed integer, and a long path or hole is one of length at least $\ell$. The authors give an algorithm deciding whether $G$ has a long odd hole (an odd hole of length at least $\ell$) in time $O(|G|^{20\ell+40})$, without trying hard to optimise the exponent. Testing for a long hole (of any parity) is easy: enumerate all induced paths of length $\ell-1$ and test whether each extends to a hole, in time $O(|G|^{\ell+1})$. Both problems are NP-hard when $\ell$ is part of the input (for long holes, subdivide each edge of an $n$-vertex graph once and take $\ell=2n$: there is a long hole if and only if the original graph is Hamiltonian; for long odd holes, take $n$ odd, subdivide every edge twice and take $\ell=3n$). The authors do not know whether either running time $|G|^{O(\ell)}$ can be substantially improved.
notes: Stated as 'We do not know if either can be substantially improved.' No formal labelled environment.
